passage: Swati won the recitation prize, and Neelam did not clap. All through the noisy bus ride home from the school trip, she whispered to the girls nearby that the judge was Swati's neighbour and that Swati's mother had written the poem. She did not know if either was true. By the time the bus stopped, the whispers had travelled to the back seat. Next morning three classmates looked at Swati strangely, and Swati sat alone. Neelam expected to feel better. Instead she could not focus on her spelling test, and her stomach hurt each time she remembered what she had said. By Friday Swati's friends had told her it was not true and the talk faded, but Neelam was still carrying the knot.

qa.q: Where did Neelam whisper the rumour?
qa.a: She whispered it during the noisy bus ride home from the school trip.

qa.q: What did Neelam believe about Swati's win, and how sure was she?
qa.a: She believed the win was unfair, but she did not know if her claims were true, so the belief came more from resentment than from facts.

qa.q: What could Neelam do to loosen the knot she was carrying?
qa.a: She could tell the girls she was not sure what she had said was true, and put that energy into practising her own recitation.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt when classmates looked at her strangely?
qa.a: Swati was probably hurt and confused after only winning a prize, and sitting alone suggests the whispers reached Swati.

grounding: Neelam believes the prize was unfair, gossips, and finds the resentment hurts her more than it hurts the winner.

passage: When Salma won the inter-school essay prize, Joseph was sure it was unfair. "Her tuition sir wrote it," he whispered to three classmates by the water cooler of their Pune school. By Friday the rumour had spread through Class 7. Salma stopped answering in class. But Joseph felt worse, not better. He kept checking who was talking about it, couldn't enjoy the cricket match on Saturday, and lay awake replaying her name being called. On Monday Salma read her essay aloud in assembly, stumbling over a line she had clearly written herself, about her Ammi's sewing machine. Joseph's ears burned. The grudge had eaten his whole weekend and hadn't changed the prize at all.

qa.q: What did Joseph whisper to three classmates?
qa.a: Joseph whispered, "Her tuition sir wrote it."

qa.q: Why did Joseph's ears burn when Salma read her essay?
qa.a: Joseph felt ashamed, realising the essay was clearly her own and his rumour was unfair.

qa.q: What could Joseph do now to repair things?
qa.a: Joseph could tell the three classmates the rumour was wrong and apologise to Salma, rather than keep carrying the grudge.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt during the week of the rumour?
qa.a: Salma probably felt hurt and embarrassed, which is why she stopped answering in class.

grounding: Illustrates a child who believes a rival's win was unfair, spreads gossip, and finds the resentment hurts him more than her.

passage:
"Swati only won the singing prize because the judge is her mother's friend."
"Who told you that?"
"Everyone knows."
"Sabina, I asked around. Nobody knows. You started it on Monday."
"Well, she can't even hold the high note properly."
"She held it for ages. We all heard."
"..."
"You've talked about Swati every break this week. You didn't even eat your paratha today."
"Because it's not fair!"
"Or because you wanted it really badly?"
"...I practised every day, Ruth."
"I know. So did she. Being angry at her isn't making you sing better. It's making you miserable."
"Maybe I should stop saying the judge thing."
"Maybe you should tell people it wasn't true."

qa.q: What did Sabina claim about the judge?
qa.a: Sabina said the judge is Swati's mother's friend.

qa.q: What does Sabina's "...I practised every day" reveal about how she feels?
qa.a: It reveals Sabina feels hurt and disappointed at losing after so much practice, and that envy lies under her anger at Swati.

qa.q: What small step would help Sabina now?
qa.a: Telling people the judge story wasn't true, as Ruth suggests, would stop the harm and free Sabina from the grudge.

qa.q: How might Swati experience the rumour if she hears it?
qa.a: Swati would likely feel hurt and insulted that her hard-won prize was called unfair.

grounding: Shows a child spreading gossip that a rival's win was unfair, and a friend helping her see the resentment hurts her most.
